    <div class="memo-content">
      <h2 id="purpose">Purpose</h2>
      <p>
        This memo evaluates Philadelphia's Digital Right-of-Way and Mobility
        Improvement Project and proposes a Stage II architecture for ROWDS:
        an evidence-based event workflow built around asset trust and
        cross-agency coordination.
      </p>
      <p>
        The proposed operating layer has two parts. The <strong>Trusted
        Asset-State Process</strong> supports ongoing asset maintenance, while
        the <strong>Standardized Event Workflow</strong> turns permits,
        closures, utility work, and related operational changes into trackable
        ROWDS events.
      </p>
      <div class="memo-callout">
        The central shift is from shared data to view toward shared process to
        operate.
      </div>

      <h2 id="current-state">Current State</h2>
      <p>
        Stage I's most important achievement was the prototype ROWDS, which
        gave Philadelphia a more granular way to represent right-of-way assets
        beyond the street-centerline level. It also established a strong
        foundation for future service expansion and cross-agency coordination.
      </p>
      <p>
        The next challenge is operational. ROWDS needs to live inside daily
        workflows and keep pace with real-world changes. Asset states still
        require a sustainable trust mechanism, especially because right-of-way
        conditions can change through permits, utility work, field inspections,
        sensors, and other operational events.
      </p>
      <p>
        Stage I also demonstrated that permit data can be converted into
        ROWDS-compliant Event Policy objects, but that process remained a
        prototype. Without a live event workflow, coordination can still fall
        back to manual map checks, email confirmation, and conversations outside
        the system.
      </p>

      <h2 id="strategy">Proposed Strategy</h2>
      <p>
        In Stage II, the evidence-based event workflow should respond directly
        to two gaps: asset trust and workflow standardization.
      </p>
      <p>
        The Trusted Asset-State Process should avoid updating ROWDS asset states
        from a single source automatically. Instead, it should define a set of
        trusted information sources, including Cityworks, permits, utility work,
        field inspections, and sensors, then standardize those signals into
        ROWDS-compatible asset-state events.
      </p>
      <p>
        Each event should carry a consistent information framework: source
        system, source record ID, timestamp, geometry, affected ROWDS asset ID,
        change type, proposed state, confidence level, and review status. A
        state resolution framework can then compare signals across sources and
        decide whether to keep an existing record, create a temporary state,
        propose a permanent asset update, or route the case to manual review.
      </p>
      <p>
        The Standardized Event Workflow should convert street closures, utility
        work, curb regulation changes, and transit disruptions into trackable
        ROWDS events. Each event should identify affected assets and route the
        case to the responsible agencies, keeping review status and decisions in
        one shared record.
      </p>

      <h2 id="pilot">Pilot Proposal</h2>
      <p>
        The proposed pilot is utility work permits that require sidewalk
        closures. This use case involves multiple agencies, temporary changes
        to right-of-way assets, and high coordination requirements, making it a
        strong test case for both TASP and SEW.
      </p>
      <p>
        When a permit enters the existing LaneClosure process, it would become a
        ROWDS event linked to the affected sidewalk segment, curb segment, and
        ADA ramp. The shared event record would route review tasks to Streets,
        the ADA coordinator, and PPA when curb or loading impacts are relevant.
      </p>
      <p>
        After agency review, the event would feed into the Trusted Asset-State
        Process as a high-confidence operational event. The system could create
        a temporary asset state without overwriting the permanent record, then
        expire that temporary state when the approved time window ends unless
        new evidence indicates a longer-term change.
      </p>

      <h2 id="evaluation">Evaluation</h2>
      <p>
        The pilot should be evaluated against reductions in off-system
        coordination, faster agency notification, improved event-to-asset
        linkage, and stronger evidence trails for future ROWDS updates.
      </p>
